top.title: Kentucky rushes for season-low in disappointing loss to Florida
top.description: Kentucky hosted the Florida Gators as its final night game of the 2026 season at Kroger Field. It was a weird, back-and-forth game in which Florida left with a win. The game was full of storylines, with transfers on both sides, but primarily involving the coaches on the Gators’ sideline. Jon Sumrall, former player and coach at Kentucky, would return to his old Kentucky home for the first time since his departure in 2022 to be the head coach at Troy. Another coach over on that sideline was Kentucky’s defensive coordinator under Mark Stoops for the final six years of his tenure in Lexington. No doubt those two would want to go back to Gainesville with a win, with both having a chip on their shoulder heading into the contest. Well, the two defensive-minded coaches got to leave with smiles on their faces after a 21-14 victory for Florida. How did they do it? Well, they stopped the run. Kentucky came into the night averaging 163.7 yards on the ground per game, and left tonight’s contest with only 61 yards. Start to finish, the Florida defense never let Kentucky get rolling at all. The offense tried everything they could to get something going, from throwing different players out there to different formations and motions, but nothing helped. Florida came in with a plan to stop Kentucky on the ground, and they executed it. CJ Baxter, Jason Patterson, Jovantae Barnes, Mikkel Skinner, Brennen Ward, and Kenny Minchey all had their chances to run the ball, and none could break through. In all honesty, Minchey may have looked the best, even though he only ended the game with one yard due to sack yards. “Didn’t establish the run tonight, at all,” Stein said about the struggling run game. “Got out-physicalled at the point of attack. That, to me, was the early indication: not being able to run the ball; you run it for 61 yards on 27 carries. And they rush it for 211 on 48; that’s a problem. We’ve gotta address it and get it fixed.” Kentucky won’t have a chance at the dream season we had all started to believe in with them dropping out of the College Football Playoff, but there’s still pride to play for, as Stein and multiple players said. Running the ball for over 100 fewer yards will help you end the season with four straight losses if you’re not careful. With a road game to Missouri on deck and a home game against Louisville following it, Kentucky’s offense has got to figure some things out in the run game. It was unacceptable against Florida and is certainly one of the more eye-opening stats when you look at how Kentucky defeated Florida.

top.title: Newark Catholic graduate Wright coaches Otterbein to OAC record
top.description: WESTERVILLE - The Otterbein volleyball team stands above the rest in the history of the Ohio Athletic Conference. Otterbein swept visiting Muskingum, 25-22, 25-10, 25-17, on Nov. 14 to win an OAC-record fifth consecutive tournament championship. The Cardinals have been coached throughout their run by Newark Catholic graduate Monica (McDonald) Wright. "Otterbein has been very good to me, and we have had tons of great girls come through the program," said Wright, who has led the Cardinals for two dominant decades shortly after starring as a player at Wittenberg. "We are in an awesome spot where we have six seniors still with the program. When you have that much experience on the floor and the tradition here - I am just super proud of them." Watkins Memorial graduate Elise Adelman piled up 32 assists and added eight kills and nine digs for Otterbein in the championship match. Adelman has played for the Cardinals the past two seasons after setting multiple program records during two seasons at Bloomsburg. "This team is something special. We've had a great season, and we are not done yet. We knew we had to battle, and we did just that," Adelman said. "As soon as I came here, something in me changed. This program, it's a family. I am so happy to be here." Lexi Scott, a Zane Trace graduate, led a a balanced attack with 12 kills to take tournament Most Outstanding Player honors. She, Adelman and Emerson Baum represented Otterbein on the all-tournament team. NC graduate Sydney Gummer totaled four kills and two assisted blocks. Gummer, who has had a standout freshman season after helping the Green Wave win the Division VI state championship a year ago, led the Muskies with 16 kills in their semifinal victory against Mount Union. Sheridan graduate Alexis Bradley, the Muskies’ setter, joined teammate Mackenzie Krous on the all-tournament team. Otterbein this week will continue their impressive season in the NCAA tournament. The Cardinals have qualified for the postseason for the 12th time in 19 seasons under Wright. "(Wright) expects the best from me every day," Adelman said. "She pushes me every day. She knows I can only get better." ksnyder@newarkadvocate.com 740-973-4541 Instagram: @newarkurt This article originally appeared on Newark Advocate: Newark Catholic graduate Wright coaches Otterbein to OAC record

top.title: ’Simply to get a…’- NFL’s latest Drake London fine sparks blunt response from J.J. Watt
top.description: Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images J.J. Watt has questioned the NFL after Atlanta Falcons wide receiver Drake London was handed another hefty fine for unnecessary roughness, with the former defensive end suggesting the league may be trying to provoke a reaction. London was fined $23,882 for using his helmet against Cincinnati Bengals cornerback DJ Turner II during the Falcons’ Week 9 game in Madrid. The latest punishment comes after London was already fined $12,537 for an incident involving Tampa Bay Buccaneers linebacker Alex Anzalone. Both violations were first-time offences in their respective categories. J.J. Watt questions NFL’s decision to fine Drake London again Watt did not hold back when reacting to the latest punishment on X, resharing NFL insider Tom Pelissero’s report. “They have to be doing this simply to get a reaction out of people sometimes… It worked. Twenty. Three. Thousand. Dollars. For this?” Watt posted. The incident occurred with seconds remaining in the third quarter against Cincinnati. After making a 21-yard reception, London lowered his head as he collided with Turner, resulting in the unnecessary roughness penalty. The two fines have now made for an expensive stretch for the Falcons receiver. According to the NFL’s rules, another helmet-related unnecessary roughness violation would see his fine increase to $47,762. London is also tied for the largest fine handed out in Week 9, alongside Seattle Seahawks linebacker Ernest Jones, who received the same $23,882 punishment. It has been a difficult campaign for the 24-year-old, who has recorded 44 catches for 692 receiving yards and one touchdown. Atlanta have also struggled, sitting at 3-6 despite London signing a contract extension that keeps him with the franchise through the 2030 season. His disciplinary issues have extended beyond the two fines, too. Earlier in the campaign, London was involved in an exchange with a fan during the Carolina Panthers game, admitting afterwards that he needed to take responsibility for his response. “I’m going to be honest here, I don’t take light to disrespect at all,” London said. “I don’t care who you are. I’m a man, too, at the end of the day. So, if you want to get on a personal level, I can get there, too, but it’s not the right thing to do. So, I got to take accountability for that, and I got to push forward and be the bigger man in some of those situations.” The NFL distributes fine money equally between NFLPA retired player support programmes, the NFL Foundation and other non-profit organisations supporting youth sports, community health and player safety. top.description: Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images Since being drafted as the first overall pick by the Las Vegas Aces in 2018, A’ja Wilson has cemented herself as one of the greatest players in the league’s history. The Aces came up short in the WNBA playoffs in 2026 but it was still a fantastic personal campaign for Wilson. She ended the regular season with the highest average across the league (26.2) ahead of Kelsey Mitchell (24.7) and Caitlin Clark (22.3). A’ja was similarly impressive in the postseason (27.5 average) and was also named the WNBA MVP for a record fifth time earlier this year. Now, while the 2027 campaign won’t begin for a while, she is almost certainly going to cement her name in the history books during it. As per Basketball Reference , the Aces star currently has 6,792 total career points in the WNBA. That puts her 11th in the all-time scoring list. However, she could break into the top 10 after just one game, as Wilson is only 11 points behind the now-retired Sue Bird, who occupies 10th place with 6,803 points. As well as Bird, A’ja could surpass 9th-place Cappie Pondexter (6,811) but may face a more difficult task when it comes to overtaking 8th. That position is held by Breanna Stewart (6,860), who is still active and will be competing with Wilson in the coming season. Meanwhile, though A’ja is a prolific points scorer, she is still some way off ever reaching the WNBA’s all-time points scorer, Diana Taurasi (10,646). nigeria.description: The Nigerian Guild of Editors (NGE) has condemned the arrest, detention and prosecution of Daniel Ojukwu, an investigative journalist with the Foundation for Investigative Journalism (FIJ), demanding his immediate release on bail. The Guild also called for a review of the criminal charges against Ojukwu and FIJ founder, Fisayo Soyombo, warning that the prosecution could undermine press freedom and discourage investigative journalism in Nigeria. Ojukwu is currently being held at the Kuje Correctional Centre, Abuja, after being arraigned on a 12-count charge bordering on alleged cyberstalking and criminal defamation. In a statement dated November 15 and signed by its President, Eze Anaba, and General Secretary, Onuoha Ukeh, the NGE said it was alarmed that a journalist was facing criminal prosecution over reports raising questions about the expenditure of public funds by the Office of the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Sustainable Development Goals. The Guild said Ojukwu’s investigation reportedly exposed an alleged payment of more than ₦147 million, approximately $109,000, to an Abuja-based restaurant for the construction of classrooms and a skills acquisition centre at a primary school in Lagos. According to the NGE, the investigation raised questions about the existence of the projects, as well as the capacity and track record of the company involved in the contract. It described the issues raised by the investigation as legitimate matters of public accountability that deserved transparent answers rather than the prosecution of the journalist who brought them to public attention. The Guild expressed particular concern that Ojukwu had been remanded in prison despite pleading not guilty to the charges, while his bail application, initially scheduled for November 12, was adjourned until December 1. It said the resort to arrest, detention and criminal prosecution over journalistic work raised concerns about the commitment of authorities to press freedom, freedom of expression and Nigerians’ constitutional right to information. The NGE recalled its opposition to the alleged use of cybersecurity laws by the police and other security agencies to harass, intimidate and bully journalists. “Investigative journalism is not a crime. Asking questions about public expenditure is not cyberstalking. Demanding accountability from public officials is not defamation,” the Guild said. It maintained that public office holders must be open to scrutiny over their management of public resources, adding that journalists should not face threats of arrest, prosecution or imprisonment for reporting alleged irregularities. nigeria.title: Nigerian property owner in US named among worst landlords after building collapse kills eight
nigeria.description: A Nigerian property owner, Olufemi Falade whose building collapsed onto an adjacent construction site in Brooklyn, New York, killing eight people, reportedly owes more than $450,000 in unpaid taxes, water bills and government fines. The property owner has also been listed six times on the New York City public advocate’s annual “Worst Landlords Watchlist” over allegations of poor property management. According to the New York Post, an examination of city records showed that Falade accumulated most of the outstanding debts through the three-storey building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue, which collapsed on Wednesday. The records indicated that he owes $170,000 in fines issued by the Department of Buildings in 2019 over improperly displayed signs, alongside $114,945 in unpaid water bills and $113,526 in property taxes dating back to 2021. Falade also reportedly owes the Internal Revenue Service $49,269 in unpaid personal federal income taxes, according to a 2010 lien, as well as another $4,316 in personal income taxes to New York State. The building, which had 98 outstanding violations with the city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development before the collapse, reportedly had a history of maintenance and safety problems. The violations included a leaking roof, defective doors, bedbug infestations and exposed electrical wiring. Records showed that complaints over the leaking roof dated back to 1976, with further violations issued as recently as this year. Falade purchased the 96-year-old property in 1999 through an entity known as Femi Realty Corp. In November 2024, he transferred ownership to another company he controls, Isolag Realty Corp, signing the deed as both seller and buyer without any money changing hands. The report also revealed that Falade was sentenced to 12 days in jail in 2006 and fined $50,000 for civil contempt after failing to address more than 1,800 violations across 12 Brooklyn buildings he owned at the time. Meanwhile, questions have emerged over the approval of excavation plans at an adjacent construction site believed to have contributed to the collapse. The New York City Department of Buildings reportedly approved the excavation plans in March for a proposed three-storey, 25,000-square-foot mixed-use development at 2625 Bedford Avenue. However, the approved plans allegedly failed to provide adequate structural reinforcement alongside the building that subsequently collapsed. Real estate attorney Massimo D’Angelo, of Blank Rome, called for improved coordination between city agencies responsible for property safety and enforcement. The move broke below Friday’s low of about $67,555 and marked the weakest level since mid-August, as weekend trading extended a selloff that has followed a stronger dollar and a fully priced December Federal Reserve rate hike. It slipped toward $71,000 by Thursday evening, then crashed to about $67,555 around midnight Eastern on Friday, its lowest level since August, before recovering toward $69,800 in the morning. entertainment.description: “Oh my God, Uwaezu! You need to hear the latest gist!” My younger sister buzzed with excitement. Though we had been living in different countries for a couple of years, we still made time to talk every single week. Unfortunately, when she called, I couldn’t talk on the phone as I had been ambushed by my kids, who were brandishing their homework and threatening to cry if I didn’t help them. As a mom herself, she immediately understood why I couldn’t continue with the conversation. I quickly made my excuses, and we laughed and hung up, promising to catch up at a more convenient time. However, that exchange got me thinking about how most millennial women have a radically different marriage and motherhood timeline from our mothers. You see, when my mother was in her early 40s, my siblings and I were in university, so she had a lot of free time during the week to spend relaxing, hanging out with her friends, and attending social events. Basically living her best life. I, on the other hand, at 40-plus, spend my days cooking pot after pot of hot meals that immediately get devoured by my ever-hungry kids, teaching my nursery school-aged kids how to count and spell, and trying but often failing to enforce a strict bedtime with yelling and threats. I constantly feel myself going underwater and have to fight for my life every single day. There are other ways motherhood has been such a hugely different experience for me than it was for my mother. Like many women of her generation, she got married right after secondary school as university education was not seen as vital. This meant that she was a teenage mother and so had more energy to spare on her kids. She also benefited from having a lot of support from domestic staff and relatives. I do not have any village supporting me with child-rearing. I have hired domestic staff in the past, but it was always one thing or another, and they ended up leaving me stranded. I also do not have youth on my side, and I have the back pain and other aches to prove it. But this experience is not unique to me. Rather than marking the occasion with another glamorous birthday celebration, Cuppy has chosen to share a more reflective portrait of her life. The film explores womanhood, ambition, identity, belonging and the ongoing process of becoming. There are tender moments, too. Viewers see Cuppy not just as a public figure, but as a daughter, sister and granddaughter. Her time with her grandmother offers an especially intimate glimpse into the affection and family ties at the heart of her story. The documentary also captures an evolution audiences may already have noticed. Her signature pink hair has given way to a new look, while faith, education and service have become increasingly central to how Cuppy speaks about her future. This is not a rejection of music, but a fuller picture of the person behind it. Her philanthropic work remains an important part of that picture. She has also established education funds at the University of Oxford, New York University and King’s College London to help students overcome financial barriers, particularly those from Africa. Alongside this work, Cuppy remains active as an international DJ, with performances at Glastonbury, Wireless Festival and Cannes Lions, as well as events during United Nations General Assembly week. At its heart, Ifeoluwa is a personal homecoming that brings together family, faith, Lagos and the experiences shaping Cuppy’s next chapter. sports.title: Kentucky rushes for season-low in disappointing loss to Florida
sports.description: Kentucky hosted the Florida Gators as its final night game of the 2026 season at Kroger Field. It was a weird, back-and-forth game in which Florida left with a win. The game was full of storylines, with transfers on both sides, but primarily involving the coaches on the Gators’ sideline. Jon Sumrall, former player and coach at Kentucky, would return to his old Kentucky home for the first time since his departure in 2022 to be the head coach at Troy. Another coach over on that sideline was Kentucky’s defensive coordinator under Mark Stoops for the final six years of his tenure in Lexington. No doubt those two would want to go back to Gainesville with a win, with both having a chip on their shoulder heading into the contest. Well, the two defensive-minded coaches got to leave with smiles on their faces after a 21-14 victory for Florida. How did they do it? Well, they stopped the run. Kentucky came into the night averaging 163.7 yards on the ground per game, and left tonight’s contest with only 61 yards. Start to finish, the Florida defense never let Kentucky get rolling at all. The offense tried everything they could to get something going, from throwing different players out there to different formations and motions, but nothing helped. Florida came in with a plan to stop Kentucky on the ground, and they executed it. CJ Baxter, Jason Patterson, Jovantae Barnes, Mikkel Skinner, Brennen Ward, and Kenny Minchey all had their chances to run the ball, and none could break through. In all honesty, Minchey may have looked the best, even though he only ended the game with one yard due to sack yards. “Didn’t establish the run tonight, at all,” Stein said about the struggling run game. “Got out-physicalled at the point of attack. That, to me, was the early indication: not being able to run the ball; you run it for 61 yards on 27 carries. And they rush it for 211 on 48; that’s a problem. We’ve gotta address it and get it fixed.” Kentucky won’t have a chance at the dream season we had all started to believe in with them dropping out of the College Football Playoff, but there’s still pride to play for, as Stein and multiple players said. Running the ball for over 100 fewer yards will help you end the season with four straight losses if you’re not careful. With a road game to Missouri on deck and a home game against Louisville following it, Kentucky’s offense has got to figure some things out in the run game. It was unacceptable against Florida and is certainly one of the more eye-opening stats when you look at how Kentucky defeated Florida.

sports.title: Newark Catholic graduate Wright coaches Otterbein to OAC record
sports.description: WESTERVILLE - The Otterbein volleyball team stands above the rest in the history of the Ohio Athletic Conference. Otterbein swept visiting Muskingum, 25-22, 25-10, 25-17, on Nov. 14 to win an OAC-record fifth consecutive tournament championship. The Cardinals have been coached throughout their run by Newark Catholic graduate Monica (McDonald) Wright. "Otterbein has been very good to me, and we have had tons of great girls come through the program," said Wright, who has led the Cardinals for two dominant decades shortly after starring as a player at Wittenberg. "We are in an awesome spot where we have six seniors still with the program. When you have that much experience on the floor and the tradition here - I am just super proud of them." Watkins Memorial graduate Elise Adelman piled up 32 assists and added eight kills and nine digs for Otterbein in the championship match. Adelman has played for the Cardinals the past two seasons after setting multiple program records during two seasons at Bloomsburg. "This team is something special. We've had a great season, and we are not done yet. We knew we had to battle, and we did just that," Adelman said. "As soon as I came here, something in me changed. This program, it's a family. I am so happy to be here." Lexi Scott, a Zane Trace graduate, led a a balanced attack with 12 kills to take tournament Most Outstanding Player honors. She, Adelman and Emerson Baum represented Otterbein on the all-tournament team. NC graduate Sydney Gummer totaled four kills and two assisted blocks. Gummer, who has had a standout freshman season after helping the Green Wave win the Division VI state championship a year ago, led the Muskies with 16 kills in their semifinal victory against Mount Union. Sheridan graduate Alexis Bradley, the Muskies’ setter, joined teammate Mackenzie Krous on the all-tournament team. Otterbein this week will continue their impressive season in the NCAA tournament. The Cardinals have qualified for the postseason for the 12th time in 19 seasons under Wright. "(Wright) expects the best from me every day," Adelman said. "She pushes me every day. sports.description: Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images J.J. Watt has questioned the NFL after Atlanta Falcons wide receiver Drake London was handed another hefty fine for unnecessary roughness, with the former defensive end suggesting the league may be trying to provoke a reaction. London was fined $23,882 for using his helmet against Cincinnati Bengals cornerback DJ Turner II during the Falcons’ Week 9 game in Madrid. The latest punishment comes after London was already fined $12,537 for an incident involving Tampa Bay Buccaneers linebacker Alex Anzalone. Both violations were first-time offences in their respective categories. J.J. Watt questions NFL’s decision to fine Drake London again Watt did not hold back when reacting to the latest punishment on X, resharing NFL insider Tom Pelissero’s report. “They have to be doing this simply to get a reaction out of people sometimes… It worked. Twenty. Three. Thousand. Dollars. For this?” Watt posted. The incident occurred with seconds remaining in the third quarter against Cincinnati. After making a 21-yard reception, London lowered his head as he collided with Turner, resulting in the unnecessary roughness penalty. The two fines have now made for an expensive stretch for the Falcons receiver. According to the NFL’s rules, another helmet-related unnecessary roughness violation would see his fine increase to $47,762. London is also tied for the largest fine handed out in Week 9, alongside Seattle Seahawks linebacker Ernest Jones, who received the same $23,882 punishment. It has been a difficult campaign for the 24-year-old, who has recorded 44 catches for 692 receiving yards and one touchdown. Atlanta have also struggled, sitting at 3-6 despite London signing a contract extension that keeps him with the franchise through the 2030 season. His disciplinary issues have extended beyond the two fines, too. Earlier in the campaign, London was involved in an exchange with a fan during the Carolina Panthers game, admitting afterwards that he needed to take responsibility for his response. “I’m going to be honest here, I don’t take light to disrespect at all,” London said. “I don’t care who you are. I’m a man, too, at the end of the day. So, if you want to get on a personal level, I can get there, too, but it’s not the right thing to do. So, I got to take accountability for that, and I got to push forward and be the bigger man in some of those situations.” The NFL distributes fine money equally between NFLPA retired player support programmes, the NFL Foundation and other non-profit organisations supporting youth sports, community health and player safety. sports.title: Wolff sees F1 history in Hamilton and Verstappen's unforgettable podium moment
sports.description: Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff believes the image of Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen lifting Kimi Antonelli onto their shoulders after his maiden Formula 1 championship triumph in Mexico will be remembered for decades. The Italian's title celebrations produced one of the most striking moments of the season, with two of Formula 1's biggest names joining forces to honour the sport's newest world champion. Hamilton and Verstappen, who finished second and third respectively, lifted Antonelli into the air during the podium celebrations , creating an image that Wolff believes perfectly captures the passing of generations in Formula 1. Speaking to the BBC, the Mercedes boss reflected on the significance of the moment and the remarkable circumstances that brought the three drivers together. "I think this is going to be the iconic photo for many decades to come. What an interesting coincidence that they finished second and third and lifted him up. It's almost like three generations of drivers. They come in like every ten years, and they had the potential future champion on their shoulders when he won his first world championship." Photo: Race Pictures Photo: Race Pictures The photograph carries particular significance given the careers of the three drivers involved. Hamilton, a seven-time world champion, represents an era in which Mercedes established itself as Formula 1's dominant force, while Verstappen subsequently emerged as the sport's leading figure during Red Bull's period of success. Antonelli's arrival at the top of Formula 1 now represents another generational shift, with the Italian achieving the ultimate prize at an early stage of his career. For Wolff, who has overseen Antonelli's development through the Mercedes junior programme, the moment also represents the culmination of years of investment in the young driver's potential. Wolff credits Antonelli's family for his success Beyond the celebrations in Mexico, Wolff also highlighted the influence of Antonelli's family in shaping the character of the newly crowned world champion. The Mercedes team principal believes the Italian's upbringing has played a crucial role in helping him handle the expectations and pressure that accompany a career at the highest level of motorsport. "His parents are really down-to-earth people. Father, racing driver, runs his own teams. They have the right values. They're humble. They're loyal. They're respectful. So, certainly a major part in making Kimi who he is today." Antonelli's father, Marco, has extensive experience in motorsport as both a driver and team owner, providing his son with a close connection to racing from an early age. That background helped Antonelli progress through karting and the junior single-seater categories before securing his opportunity with Mercedes.

More Videos Haaland, 26, scored an 88th-minute penalty in Norway's 3-1 UEFA Nations League win over Wales on Saturday night, after Antonio Nusa and Andreas Schjelderup had put the hosts in control in the second half. An independent commission found Manchester City guilty on 114 of 115 charges relating to the nine seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18, in a verdict published on 29 September that found the club's revenues had been inflated and its costs reduced by more than £900 million. City declared their innocence on the day of the ruling and lodged a comprehensive appeal at 7pm on 1 October, with the hearing reported to be scheduled for mid-December and any sanctions not expected until next year. This is a question I struggle to answer, says Haaland in defiant response to Man City guilty verdict Speaking to TV 2 Sport after the win over Wales, Haaland was asked about the verdict as the Manchester City number nine finally addressed the elephant in the room. The Leeds-born striker said: "It didn't start until 2009-2018, so 2009, I think I played for Bryne FK in 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013. Should we continue? "So this is a question I struggle to answer. It's a legal battle; I don't know how to say it in Norwegian. It's a case between the Premier League and Manchester City , which will be brought up with a panel and such. "Should I answer this? I don't know. We had a lot of Norwegians in the club at that time. But it's a bit of a difficult case to answer when I don't really know that much." Haaland came through the youth ranks at his hometown club Bryne before moving on to Molde, Red Bull Salzburg and Borussia Dortmund ahead of his switch to the Etihad Stadium in the summer of 2022. The Norway international added: "I don't know when the answer will be; I haven't read much about it, to be honest. "I'm focused on trying to perform for Manchester City, a club I signed a five-year contract with in 2022, and a nine-and-a-half-year contract with at the end of 2024. So I think that's really about it. I'm a City player, and I'm incredibly happy about that." Haaland's commitment to Man City and the case so far Haaland's current contract was confirmed in January 2025 and runs until 2034, with Spanish outlet Sport having previously reported that the deal does not contain a release clause tied to relegation or any other circumstance. technology.title: LEO gets a birthday bash, 75 years after clocking in
technology.description: Business computing turns 75 this month, and Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is throwing a party for LEO, the machine that helped start it all. The LEO@75 event takes place on Saturday, November 28, from 10am to 5pm, with film screenings, historical displays, and hands-on activities for children. The Register has written about the Centre for Computing History a few times. It's an interactive computer museum just off Coldhams Lane in Cambridge, and back in 2018 it won National Lottery funding to help it "preserve, archive and digitise a range of LEO Computers artefacts, documents and personal memories." Admission supports the museum charity, with student and concession tickets at £10 and family tickets starting at £15. As well as stuff for the grown-ups, including a film screening, it will include events for smaller children (5-7) and a Python coding event for older (12-16) kids. Regular readers might recall our story about the Lyons Electronic Office back in 2021, celebrating its 70th anniversary. The Reg also published an obituary for Mary Coombs, the first female commercial programmer the following year. Coombs started programming LEO in 1952. Both stories offer more on the machine and the people behind it. LEO was an early computer, but from three-quarters of a century away, it's easy to miss just how early. Its design was based on Cambridge University's EDSAC, developed by a team led by the late, great Sir Maurice Wilkes. The Reg mentioned EDSAC in our obituary for Wilkes, and went into more detail for his centenary in 2013 . It also crops up in our Geek's Guide to Cambridge . The design of EDSAC was directly inspired by John von Neumann's famous, and incomplete, "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" – which The Reg talked about in 2011 . The draft report was circulated in 1945, based on the proposal for EDVAC, four years before the hardware was delivered. That was also the year John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert completed its predecessor, ENIAC. In its original form, ENIAC was programmed by setting switches and reconnecting cables; EDVAC, by contrast, was designed to store its instructions in memory. The report set out what's now called the "von Neumann architecture." Wilkes and Douglas Hartree drew on those ideas in developing EDSAC, LEO's immediate forerunner and one of the world's earliest practical stored-program computers. The first working electronic stored-program machine was the Manchester "Baby," the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, which ran its first program in 1948 . EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949 – a few months before the delivery of BINAC, Eckert and Mauchly's first stored-program machine. LEO ran its first commercial application in 1951. That was also the year the US Census Bureau took delivery of Eckert and Mauchly's UNIVAC I . ®

science.title: 'Alien: Fireteam Elite 2' is a good old-fashioned bug hunt, ironically plagued by bugs
science.description: The first Aliens: Fireteam Elite was among my favorite Alien video games , and there were a lot of reasons to be excited for a sequel. At Summer Game Fest 2026 , we learned of many smart changes and improvements to the formula, and I was eager to go bug-hunting again. A new campaign, fully reworked classes, and four-player co-op. What could go wrong? Months later, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2's debut has been difficult, mostly due to glaring tech issues. Despite this, it's still a welcome jolt of action for a franchise that's been focusing on making the Xenomorphs scary again in recent years. Alien: Romulus (2024) and Alien: Earth (2025) have reestablished the acid-blooded Xenomorphs as bona fide horror icons, while games like Aliens: Dark Descent bet on tense real-time tactics and squad management; Rogue Incursion spooked VR and non-VR players alike; and we even have Isolation 2 's pure survival horror to look forward to. Rough edges aside, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a necessary return to mindless shooting and treating the Xenos as a relentless horde, dropping the stalking and slasher-inspired murders in favor of sci-fi shootouts and macho one-liners. It's far from a novel idea — even the original game is only five years old — but a classic for a reason. Another glorious day in the Corps (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) Believe it or not, another colony has fallen prey to the Xenomorphs in Fireteam Elite 2. The familiar setup takes a new team of Colonial Marines to a mining facility on LV-558, where contact has been lost with the first wave of Marines that went in to deal with the threat. This isn't first contact; the Marines are more than used to bug hunts by now, which means there's less exposition to cut through before getting to the Xeno-blasting chaos. The writing certainly won't stun the Academy (and there's definitely too much of it in between missions), but the agility here is appreciated. We've fought these aliens many, many times before. Fireteam Elite 2 is smart enough to sidestep fake tension and just hit the ground running. (Image credit: Daybreak Game Company) All the design changes and upgrades reinforce the intent to make the ultimate Aliens action game. Classes have more defined roles and access to better, more destructive sci-fi weapons, and the upgrade to four-player fireteams is welcome when aliens and hostile synths won't stop pouring in. Tired of replaying campaign missions on higher difficulties and with modifiers? Prepare for the worst in this shooter's version of the classic horde mode. At its best, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 understands why James Cameron's masterpiece still holds up. During the biggest Xenomorph onslaughts — when the bullets are flying and acid is spraying — the game's shortcomings and jankier elements fade away. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
science.description: null On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier. The Apollo 12 moonwalkers also performed a lot of moon science. The astronauts picked up 75 pounds of moon rocks. Most of the rocks were basalts that formed from molten lava. These basalts showed the Apollo 12 landing site is more than 3 billion years old. The Apollo 12 astronauts on NASA's second crewed moon landing mission. They are (left to right) are Charles Conrad Jr., Richard F. Gordon Jr., and Alan L. Bean. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered Apollo 12 proved that the Apollo 11 moon landing was not just a one-off stunt while setting the stage for even more ambitious missions. To truly explore the moon and advance our understanding of how our solar system formed, the follow-on Apollo flights needed to be able to land where the geologists had identified as areas of interest. Apollo 12, with its touchdown in proximity to the Surveyor probe, proved this was possible. The Apollo 12 astronauts visited NASA's Surveyor 3 lander and took samples of it back to Earth. (Image credit: NASA) The launch of Apollo 12 also underscored the importance of having a well-prepared Mission Control team, an asset that would be critical to outcome of the next mission, Apollo 13. The ability to recover from a complete electrical short out with the simple call of a through of a switch "SCE to AUX" proved that knowing every detail about how the spacecraft worked was key to a successful program. science.title: 'Now everything changes': SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for 1st time ever (video)
science.description: null SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission plan called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket . That didn't happen; Starship's Super Heavy booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship succeeded in its attempt, notching a huge milestone for SpaceX and its dream of full rocket reuse. "That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast today, his voice thick with emotion. "That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship, and now everything changes." SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), a landmark achievement that could unlock the giant vehicle's immense potential. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Space.com) The Ship catch occurred today at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT; 3:20 p.m. local Texas time), roughly 22.5 hours after Flight 15 lifted off. Many SpaceX employees went outside to watch the vehicle, known as Ship 42, descend through the clouds toward its Starbase launch tower, which the company calls "Mechazilla." And they got quite a show: Ship 42 nestled gently into Mechazilla's waiting arms, while "Baby Come Back" played over SpaceX's landing webcast. "This is so incredible to see," SpaceX's Jessie Anderson said during the livestream. "One of the most incredible and historic engineering feats of all time has just happened right in front of our eyes." Why was this such a big deal? SpaceX had already caught Super Heavy — on three previous Starship test flights, in fact. But it had never tried before with Ship. The upper stage is a tougher target, for it flies higher, farther and faster than the booster. Indeed, on Flight 15, Ship 42 came all the way back down from orbit. Ship 42 comes in for its landing on Nov. 14, 2026. science.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
science.description: null Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth . The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years , when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse. Jupiter, Mars and Regulus will appear close together on the night of Nov. 15-16. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.) Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus , which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun . A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant , formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams. How to measure distances in the night sky using your outstretched hand. (Image credit: Created in Canva Pro) Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA . Interested in seeing and capturing the planets for yourself? Then be sure to read our guide on everything you need to observe and photograph the planets of the solar system, along with our picks of the top telescopes , cameras and lenses for exploring the night sky in 2026. science.title: New Scientist readers on how the magazine has shaped their lives
science.description: Have you been reading New Scientist since the start? Getty Images/Westend61 The first issue of New Scientist was published on 22 November 1956, and some of our readers have been with us since the very beginning. We asked subscribers, young and old, to tell us how they first encountered the magazine and how New Scientist has influenced their lives. The volume of responses and the gratitude expressed within them were quite overwhelming. Here are some of our favourites, featuring a spectacular maggot experiment, science-inspired poetry and even a match made on the short-lived New Scientist dating site. Huge thanks to everyone who wrote in. I was interested to see that New Scientist was launched “for all those men and women who are interested in scientific discovery and in its industrial, commercial and social consequences”. At the age of 13, I saved up a shilling from my Saturday morning “jobs” to purchase the first edition on 22 November 1956 and became one of those people interested in scientific discovery. Seventy years later, I remain a subscriber, after a scientific career that took me to many (if not, most!) countries in the world. New Scientist covered things like the opening of Jodrell Bank telescope in 1957. Since that was only about 50 miles (80 kilometres) away, it necessitated a bike ride to see what it really looked like! Peter Hall Advertisement I seem to have been reading New Scientist for the full 70! I do recall my encounter with the first edition: I was at Bec Grammar School in south London in a second-year physics class – it was 1956. The teacher, a genial boffin-type, announced the advent of the new publication and handed out copies – all I remember is its grey (or was it beige?) pages, which I read in a perfunctory way (I was only 12!) little thinking it would follow me through life and around the globe. Robyn Williams I was at Malvern College in England for my O level examinations from 1955 to 1958. My science master at Malvern had recognised my interest in science and technology and he bought the very first issue of New Scientist with his own money. At the next science class, he stood up in front of the whole class and waved the first issue, saying, “Young Inman, a new UK science and technology magazine has been published and here is the first issue for you.” I went on to reach 60 years as a member of the UK Institution of Civil Engineers. Peter Inman 1956 puts me back at school – Fettes College in Edinburgh. The school adopted New Scientist from its first edition and it was available in the library, where senior boys interested in science were recommended to read it. And so began a lifetime of New Scientist – I have been a regular for as long as I can remember and a subscriber for a very long time. I am very grateful to New Scientist for maintaining my interest in all the sciences and new developments, which I am sure has helped me to think laterally and to have a greater understanding of what makes everything tick. science.title: SpaceX launches Starship on ambitious 22-hour Flight 15 test, but aborts booster 'chopsticks' catch (video)
science.description: null STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch. Following stage separation, Super Heavy reoriented for a planned return to Starbase as Ship powered its way toward low Earth orbit (LEO). SpaceX originally planned to catch Super Heavy with the Starbase launch tower's giant mechanical "chopstick" arms. But it wasn't to be: The company called off the catch attempt and brought the booster down for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch, for reasons that were not immediately clear. A successful catch would have been a significant milestone for SpaceX and its efforts to design Starship as a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. It would have been the first successful recovery of a Version 3 (V3) Super Heavy , which SpaceX began flying earlier this year. The company previously recovered three of its V1 Super Heavy vehicles and reused two of those in later flights. SpaceX's Starship megarocket launches on its 15th test flight from Starbase, Texas on Nov. 13, 2026. (Image credit: Future/Josh Dinner, Space.com) Ship goes to orbit Ship's Raptors continued to fire following stage separation, completing their first burn just after eight minutes into flight. All went according to plan after that for Ship as well: A second engine burn lasting about 20 seconds parked Ship in LEO at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) at T+26 minutes and 10 seconds. "We’ve got a nominal orbit insertion, so Starship now in orbit around Earth for the second time ever," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during today's Flight 15 launch webcast. "That’s a really great moment." Ship first reached orbit on Flight 14 , which launched on Sept. 28. Ship carried 26 of SpaceX's Starlink V3 spacecraft, which were deployed into LEO on schedule today over a 42-minute span starting 35 minutes after launch. The upgraded wireless internet satellites are the second V3 batch to reach orbit, after a set of 26 that were delivered on Flight 14 . science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 13, 1971: NASA's Mariner 9 becomes 1st spacecraft to orbit Mars, revealing close looks at the Martian surface
science.description: null On Nov. 13, 1971, Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars. At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. When Mariner 9 got to Mars , it arrived in the middle of a dust storm. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona. Mariner 9 worked for one year in orbit. When it ran out of gas, NASA shut it off. But the spacecraft remains one of the most famous Mars voyagers of all time. The Mariner 9 spacecraft, seen here in a NASA model, was the first to orbit Mars in 1971. (Image credit: NASA) Here's why it mattered Mariner 9 cemented its place in space history when it entered into orbit around Mars, the first human-built spacecraft ever to do so. The NASA spacecraft actually beat the Soviet Union's own Mars 2 spacecraft to the Red Planet, even though Mars 2 "had an 11-day head start," NASA said in a mission description . (Mars 2 would go on to be the first human-built craft to impact the surface of Mars when it crashed into the Red Planet.) But it was the science from Mariner 9 that transformed Mars from a mysterious Red Planet into a full world for humans to explore. The Boldest Mars Missions in History The Mariner 9 mission first saw the peak of Olympus Mons on Mars in the midst of a global dust storm in 1971. (Image credit: NASA/JPL) Mariner 9 carried four primary instruments to study Mars, including a camera system for imaging, an ultraviolet spectrometer, an infrared spectrometer and an infrared radiometer. The probe mapped 85% of Mars with those tools during its nearly one-year mission. The Mariner 9 spacecraft discovered 20 giant volcanoes on Mars (including Olympus Mars) and made key observations to map Valles Marineris, which runs 2,500 miles (4,000 kilometers) long acros the Tharsis region and is 120 miles (200 km) wide. "The canyon was named in honor of Mariner 9," NASA said in an overview . In all, Mariner 9 took 7,329 photos of the surface of Mars, mapping the planet down to a resolution of between 1/2-1 mile (1-2 km). It also snapped at least 80 photos of Phobos and Deimos, the two small moons of Mars. By February 1972, Mariner 9's supply of gaseous nitrogen, which it used to feed its attitide control thrusters, had run dry. NASA finally shut down the mission in October 1972. science.title: 60 years ago the Leonid meteor shower produced 144,000 meteors per hour. Could it happen again?
science.description: null This year marks a rather auspicious anniversary for meteor watchers. Sixty years ago , one of the most stupendous Leonid meteor displays lit up the predawn skies over the central and western U.S. So, what will the 2026 Leonids bring us? And what might they bring in the years to come? The Leonid meteor shower is one of the most celebrated of the year's annual displays of "shooting stars." The mere mention of the Leonids usually elicits mental images of a sky filled with shooting stars pouring down through the sky like rain. Such meteor storms have indeed occurred with the Leonids, such as in 1833 and 1966 when meteor rates of tens of thousands per hour were observed. In more recent years, most notably 1999 , 2001 and 2002 , lesser Leonid displays of up to "only" a few thousand meteors per hour took place. Unfortunately, that's not likely to be the case this year. In fact, comparatively speaking, this is going to be a lean year for the Leonids chiefly because of the expected lack of any significant activity. Although the Leonids are one of the most famous of all the annual meteor displays, this year they're not likely to be very productive. It's probable they are going to be rather weak and there probably will be long stretches when not a single Leonid will be seen. I'll explain why in a moment. First, let's find out about this shower's lineage. What causes the Leonids? The Leonids are so named because the shower's radiant point, from where the meteors seem to fan out, is located within the constellation of Leo the Lion, from the backward question mark pattern of stars known as " The Sickle." The meteors are caused by the Tempel-Tuttle comet , which sweeps through the inner solar system every 33⅓ years. Each time the comet passes closest to the sun it leaves a "river of rubble" in its wake: a dense trail of dusty debris. A meteor storm becomes possible if the Earth were to score a direct hit on a fresh dust trail ejected by the comet over the past several centuries. The "lion's share" (no pun intended) of comet dust can be found just ahead and trailing behind Tempel-Tuttle. That comet last swept through the inner solar system in 1998. That's why spectacular meteor showers were seen in 1999, 2001 and 2002, with declining numbers thereafter. The most famous depiction of the 1833 Leonids, actually produced in 1888 for the Adventist book Bible Readings for the Home Circle . The engraving is by Adolf Vollmy based upon an original painting by the Swiss artist Karl Jauslin, that is in turn based on a first-person account of the 1833 storm by a minister, Joseph Harvey Waggoner on his way from Florida to New Orleans. science.title: 100 launches! Rocket Lab sends Earth-observing satellite to orbit on milestone mission (photos)
science.description: null Rocket Lab just hit the century mark. An Electron rocket topped with a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite lifted off from Rocket Lab's New Zealand site on Saturday (Nov. 14) at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT; 6:30 p.m. local New Zealand time). The mission, which Rocket Lab called "The Mountain God Rises," was a big one: It marked the 100th launch to date for the California-based company. The first stage of Rocket Lab's Electron rocket falls back to Earth during "The Mountain God Rises" mission on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) Rocket Lab launched for the first time in May 2017, sending the brand-new Electron up on a test flight from New Zealand. That effort failed, but Electron bounced back on its second-ever liftoff, delivering several cubesats to low Earth orbit (LEO) in January 2018. In the years since, the 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron has become one of the most prolific and reliable rockets in the world, carrying small payloads to the final frontier for a variety of customers. And it hit the century mark on Saturday in record-breaking fashion: No commercially developed rocket has gotten there faster, not even SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9 , according to Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck. "It's an unprecedented milestone for a commercial small-lift orbital rocket, and a threshold rarely crossed in modern spaceflight," Beck said on Monday (Nov. 9), during Rocket Lab's third-quarter earnings call with investors. "But what matters most to us and our customers is that we have achieved a 96% reliability rate across 99 launches." Electron met the moment in style on Saturday morning, thanks to some fancy livery. "Black rocket 🤝 Golden milestone. Electron is all dressed up for launch 100," Rocket Lab said via X on Tuesday (Nov. 10), in a post that shared a photo of the specially painted first stage. Not all of Rocket Lab's missions have gone orbital, it should be noted: A suborbital variant of Electron known as HASTE , which customers use to test technologies in a hypersonic flight environment, has nine missions under its belt to date. The Electron rocket that flew Rocket Lab's 100th mission sported some special livery. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) "The Mountain God Rises" was Rocket Lab's 11th launch to date for the Tokyo-based company iQPS, which is building a constellation of three dozen synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites in LEO. And all went to plan on the mission: Electron's upper "kick stage" deployed a single iQPS spacecraft 357 miles (575 kilometers) above Earth. SAR satellites can see through cloud cover and image our planet at night as well as during the day, offering key advantages over spacecraft that are optimized to view in optical wavelengths. science.title: California's brand-new Air & Space Center, home of the space shuttle Endeavour, opens today
science.description: null LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13). After more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour , sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall. "It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour. The space shuttle Endeavour. (Image credit: Olivia Hemaratanatorn/Future) "There are people that come from all over the world, and when they come to Los Angeles, they're going to have the opportunity to see it, too," Reisman added. "The exposure it's going to have is just a force multiplier. There are so many people that can have that opportunity to bring their kids here and show them [the shuttle] and have that experience." Entering into this exhibit is an experience in and of itself, as I can personally attest; I was among of group of reporters who got a sneak peek at the new wing on Oct. 28. A video presentation ends in a dramatic reveal: Visitors walk into a space where the enormous shuttle, which flew 25 missions to Earth orbit from 1992 to 2011, feels truly larger than life. The new Endeavour exhibit features a replica launch tower, from which you can look down at the shuttle. (Image credit: Future) There are a number of interactive exhibits around the base of Endeavour, which you can slide down to (though, of course, you can also take the elevator or stairs). From a shuttle landing simulator to a replica of a shuttle cockpit that you can sit in, to shuttle tires and space tech from across decades of spaceflight history, there's an incredible variety of space artifacts to both observe and interact with. As for Endeavour itself: It is open, so you can peer inside to see the robotic arm tucked away among a myriad of handles, straps and electronic gear inside. science.title: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
science.description: null Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars. In fact, you're likely to catch their collective brightness in your peripheral vision every time you go outside and look up. But every November the Pleiades remind me that naked-eye observing isn't as simple as opening the back door and looking up. How many Pleiades I can see can change depending on what I do during the next 10 minutes. What's happening and when to look You can easily see the Pleiades as a bright misty patch in your peripheral vision during winter. (Image credit: Haitong Yu via Getty Images) The Pleiades, also known as Messier 45 (M45) or the "Seven Sisters," are an open star cluster in Taurus. They're one of the closest clusters to the solar system and some of the youngest stars you can see with the naked eye — just 100 million years old. They're basically newborns. In mid-November, they rise in the east in the early evening and climb higher as the night progresses, making this an excellent time to get acquainted with them. Look east after dark for a tiny, compact group of stars. If you know Orion, which rises later, the Pleiades are above and to the right of it from mid-northern latitudes. Nearby you'll also find orange Aldebaran and the much broader V-shaped Hyades cluster. The Hyades are closer to the sun , but their stars are about 625 million years old. The name "Seven Sisters" creates an immediate observational trap: people assume they're supposed to see seven stars. That's not necessarily true. In fact, six is a common naked-eye result under decently dark conditions (note that the shape of the six brightest is like a mini Big Dipper /Plough), while people with sharp eyesight under darker skies may see more. The cluster itself contains about 1,000 stars. The number you personally distinguish depends on eyesight, sky brightness, atmospheric conditions and how well your eyes have adapted to darkness. science.title: 'Martian Isolation' is an upcoming sci-fi survival horror game that looks like 'The Martian' and 'Event Horizon' had a horrific child
science.description: null "Martian Isolation" is an upcoming single-player, first-person survival horror game that's just been revealed with a suitably creepy launch trailer. And yes, it does look an awful lot like " The Martian ," doesn't it? There's a lot of survival gameplay on display here that mirrors Mark Watney's tale of survival on the Red Planet, as your stranded protagonist is forced to explore the Martian surface to acquire resources, grow plants, and repair their base. That comparison to Andy Weir's sci-fi masterpiece does fall away as you get further into the trailer, though, when the horror part of the game's description comes into play: Flickering lights, creepy figures stalking the halls of your Martian habitat, and blood dripping from the walls. Oh yeah, that's some good creepy sci-fi horror right there. It's giving " Event Horizon ", and that's always getting a thumbs-up from me. There's no release date scheduled at this time, with the 'Martian Isolation' Steam page simply listing it as "coming soon," though the YouTube trailer description does say it "will be available on Steam in 2027". You can't pre-order yet, but if this looks like your jam, you can add it to your wishlist. Beyond that, we know shockingly little about this title. It's the debut game from Golden Milestone Studio, but there's very little information out there beyond a name. The latest blog post on the game's Steam page says that they're a "small team," but what we've seen so far is encouraging. There seems to be a pronounced split between the survival and horror elements of the game along the day/night cycle. Daytime sees you exploring the Martian surface, smashing rocks, cleaning solar panels, and doing sick jumps on a quad bike. The psychological torment only begins once the sun goes down (they mostly come out at night … mostly), as your character starts encountering cosmic horrors and weird naked zombie men. Nope, nope, nope, I'm out! Golden Milestone Studio Are they hallucinations, or is there some malevolent presence hiding in the blood-red sands of Mars ? I'm always looking for new ways to shatter my psyche and possibly soil my pants, so I'll be keeping a close eye on this one. In the meantime, I do need to get back and finish " Routine ." I left my character hiding under a desk months ago, and I haven't been brave enough to go back. As Mama always said, you can't have any Martian horror until you finish your lunar horror first.
